# An anecdote {.unnumbered}

Which map took you the longest to make?

![Source: Ipea, [repositorio.ipea.gov.br/handle/11058/10713](https://repositorio.ipea.gov.br/handle/11058/10713).](../img/map_years_BR21.png)

This is my answer. Analysing how the motorisation rate changed in every Brazilian city looks simple. On
paper, it is. There are two sources: population, from IBGE, and the vehicle fleet, from Denatran. Two tables,
one division. I expected to finish it in an afternoon.

The first obstacle was downloading the data. Denatran publishes the fleet split by
year and by month, each slice in its own file. That meant hundreds of manual downloads.
I wrote code to automate it. But the files followed no pattern at all: the address for
2001 was not the one for 2010, which was not the one for 2020. I ended up with a download routine
for each year. The automation I had written to save time became a small project of its
own.

Then came the population data, and with them a subtler trap: some years have count data, others
have projections. These are numbers of different natures, and putting them in the same
series requires knowing that. Nothing in the file warns you.

But what really ate up the time was matching the two datasets. Denatran's old tables
had no municipality code: only the city name, typed in, decade after decade. And a Brazilian
city name is not a reliable key. I standardised everything: removed accents, cedillas, hyphens,
letter case. Even so, the matching kept failing. Paraty appears with a "y" in one dataset and with
an "i" in the other. Old spellings with "ph" that current rules no longer use. Connectives such as "de",
"do" and "da" appeared in one file and were missing in the other. Municipalities that changed name,
became independent or merged in the meantime.

There was no shortcut. I had to build by hand a lookup table linking each historical
spelling to the current IBGE code. And the only way to know whether it was making progress was
visual: I plotted the map of each state highlighting the municipalities with no match and
watched the holes close. The map was my debugging tool.

That took days. Producing the final chart in R took one or two more. Testing colour palettes and
typography until the figure was readable took the rest of the week.

I tell this story for two reasons. The first is that the heavy lifting in data analysis is almost
never in the modelling. It is in making two datasets talk to each other. The second is what this story
teaches about checking: a badly resolved `join` does not throw an error. It runs, returns a table, and
you move on without knowing that you lost three hundred municipalities along the way, or that you duplicated
rows and inflated your totals. The result looks nice and is wrong.

Throughout the course, whenever we integrate datasets, we will repeat the same discipline: check the
row count before and after the `join`, look at what was left out, compare the aggregate with the
official source.
